title: Dark Days and White Nights
blurb: Talk about different climates and lifestyles

steps.html:
Sixty days when the sun does not rise, and sixty when it does not set. The people who live through both say the dark half is the easy one — which takes some explaining.

  • Read two accounts of an extreme climate
  • Form and place adjectives and adverbs accurately
  • Describe how climate shapes the way people live
  • Write about the climate where you are

Sixty days without a sunrise
steps.html:
Reading 1 · 146 words

In Tromsø, four hundred kilometres inside the Arctic Circle, the sun basically does not appear for sixty days. Norwegians call it the polar night. Visitors call it depressing, usually before they have been through one.

The reality is stranger than that. It does not go completely dark. For four or five hours in the middle of the day the sky turns a deep, artificial-looking blue, and everything under it — snow, buildings, the mountainside above the town — takes that colour on. People who have lived through several of them describe it as magical rather than miserable, and they say it slightly irritably, because they are tired of being asked.

What changes is not mood but rhythm. Nobody wakes up automatically. Lights go on considerably earlier and stay on considerably longer, and the town gets gradually quieter through January in a way that has nothing to do with unhappiness.

steps.title: What does the writer say changes during the polar night?
options: People's mood, which becomes noticeably worse.
People's rhythm — when they wake, when the lights go on, how busy the town is.
steps.answer: People's rhythm — when they wake, when the lights go on, how busy the town is.
steps.why: 'What changes is not mood but rhythm.' The last paragraph then lists what that means in practice.

steps.title: And then it does not get dark at all
steps.html:
Reading 2 · 148 words

The other half of the year is harder to explain to anybody who has not seen it. From late May the sun does not properly set. It drops towards the horizon at about one in the morning, turns everything a warm orange, and comes back up.

This is not a small difference. The contrast between the two extremes is dramatic, and it exists because of the tilt of the Earth's axis rather than anything local. Tromsø is on roughly the same latitude as northern Alaska.

People behave differently, and they know they do. Gardens get dug at midnight. Children are cheerfully impossible to put to bed. A friend of mine, originally from Pakistan and now permanently in Norway, says the white nights unsettle her far more than the dark ones ever did — the darkness is cosy, and the light will not let you stop.

The sun drops towards the horizon and comes back up without setting.

steps.answer: The sun drops towards the horizon and comes back up without setting.
steps.why: 'It drops towards the horizon at about one in the morning… and comes back up.'

steps.title: Which word describes which
steps.html:
Formation, position, and the three places learners lose marks.

An adjective describes a noun. An adverb describes a verb, an adjective, or another adverb. A dramatic contrast — adjective. The light returns gradually — adverb.

Most adverbs are the adjective plus -ly, with three spelling rules: -y → -ily (happy → happily), -le → -ly (gradual… simple → simply), -ic → -ically (dramatic → dramatically, automatic → automatically, basic → basically).

Some words are the same in both jobs: fast, hard, late, early, daily. And watch hard / hardly and late / lately — hardly means 'almost not', and lately means 'recently'. They are not the adverbs of hard and late.

After the verbs be, look, feel, seem, sound, taste, smell, become, get, use an adjective, not an adverb: It looks strange, not looks strangely.

Position: adverbs of degree go before the word they modify (considerably warmer, slightly darker); adverbs of manner usually go after the verb and its object (she said it irritably). Never place an adverb between a verb and its object: I like very much this town.

-ic → -ically.

After be, an adjective.

After an ordinary verb, an adverb.

Children are cheerfully impossible.
Adverb before an adjective.

It turns everything a warm orange.

She is permanently in Norway now.
Adverb modifying the whole clause.

steps.title: Deciding between the adjective and the adverb
steps.html:
1. The sentence: The town gets ___ (quiet) through January.
  2. Ask what the word describes. It describes the town, not the getting. That means an adjective: The town gets quiet.
  3. This is because get belongs with be, look, feel, seem, become — verbs that link a subject to a description rather than to an action.
  4. Now add the degree word: The town gets gradually quieter. Here gradually is an adverb modifying the adjective quieter.
  5. Compare an ordinary verb: The town empties gradually. Empties is an action, so the adverb attaches to it directly.

steps.title: Write your description.
steps.sub: 140–170 words. Use at least four adverbs and at least four adjectives, and make sure each is doing the right job.
steps.html:
• Open with what outsiders assume, and correct it.
  • Say what actually changes, using <i>What changes is not … but …</i>
  • Describe how people behave, with at least two adverbs.
  • Close with a contrast, using an adjective after <i>be</i>.

Useful language

  • Visitors call it … , usually before they have been through one.
  • It gets considerably / slightly / gradually …
  • What changes is not … but …
  • The contrast between … and … is dramatic.
  • People behave differently, and they know they do.
  • It looks / feels / seems …
steps.modelHtml:
February in Karagandy

Outsiders assume the cold is the problem. It is not. Minus thirty is dry, bright and perfectly manageable once you own the right coat, and the sky in February is a deep, almost artificial blue.

What changes is not the temperature but the light. It goes dark at half past four, which means the whole second half of the day happens indoors, under artificial light, and the town gets gradually quieter from about the middle of January.

People behave differently and they know they do. Nobody arranges anything for a February evening. Everybody eats considerably more than they need. The contrast with June, when it is still light at ten and the courtyards are full until midnight, is dramatic enough to feel like two separate cities.
